opus-5.5.text:
I think it's possible, but maybe not in the way people usually imagine. When people say "one model that does everything," they often picture something like AlphaGo scaled up: you define a reward, run RL long enough, and the model becomes superhuman at every task. I don't think that's quite how it will play out.

What has changed recently is that RL finally generalizes. For a long time, RL was about training one agent for one environment, like Atari or Go, and it didn't transfer. Now, because of language pretraining, we have strong priors. Language gives the model a way to reason and to think before it acts, and that reasoning is the part that generalizes. When you do RL on top of that prior, on math, on coding, on some agent tasks, you see gains that carry over to things you never trained on. So technically, a single model getting better across many tasks through RL is already happening.

The harder question is what "all tasks" means. Math and coding have clean, verifiable rewards. Most real-world tasks don't. Helping someone run a business, doing research, or being a good assistant over weeks of interaction involves long horizons, fuzzy goals, and many people with different preferences. The bottleneck isn't the RL algorithm anymore. It's the environments, the evaluations, and how we define reward for messy, open-ended tasks. That's why I've argued we're entering a "second half," where defining the problem matters more than the method.

There's also a question of utility versus capability. A single general model might be very capable, but to be useful for a particular person or company, it needs context and memory: who you are, what you've done before, what your organization cares about. So I'd guess the future is a strong general model at the core, with RL giving broad reasoning and agentic ability, plus a lot of personalization and context on top. Whether you call that "one model" is partly semantic.

So my short answer is yes, RL can push toward a much more general model than we had before. But the hard part isn't scaling the training. It's building the right tasks and rewards for the real world, and that's where I think the interesting work is now.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts tasks with clean, verifiable rewards and messy, open-ended goals, but does not state that reasoning transfer itself depends on the nature of the tasks.

r002.rationale: It says a single model getting better across many tasks through RL is already happening and concludes that RL can push toward a much more general model.

r003.rationale: It says RL on language pretraining across math, coding, and agent tasks produces gains that carry over to tasks the model was never trained on.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's possible, but I'd separate two questions that often get mixed together: can one model do all tasks, and can reinforcement learning be the thing that gets us there.

On the first question, I'm actually fairly optimistic. The history of this field is basically a history of unification. We used to have a different model for every NLP task, then we had one pretrained model with a different head for each task, then with GPT-3 we had one model and just different prompts. Each step, people said "this specialized thing will never be absorbed by the general thing," and each time it was. So the prior should be that generalization keeps winning.

The second question is harder, and this is where I think people are a little too excited right now. RL has always worked well when you have a clean environment and a clean reward. Atari, Go, and now things like math and code, where you can verify the answer. The reason RL suddenly looks like it generalizes is not that the algorithms got dramatically better. It's that the prior got dramatically better. You're not starting from a random policy anymore; you're starting from a language model that already has the world knowledge and the language. So RL is doing something closer to shaping behavior than learning from scratch.

The problem is that most of the tasks humans actually care about don't come with a verifier. If I ask you to write a good research proposal, or run a company, or have a useful conversation with a user over three months, what's the reward? You can't just check an answer. So when people say "RL will give us one model for everything," I'd ask: where do the environments come from, and where do the rewards come from? Those are the real bottlenecks now, more than the model architecture or the algorithm.

I've been calling this the second half of AI. In the first half, the hard part was the methods: the Transformer, pretraining, scaling. The benchmarks were sort of given. Now the methods are relatively settled, and the hard part is defining the tasks. What should the model be evaluated on? What does it mean to "do a task well" in an open-ended setting? Whoever figures out how to build environments and rewards for the messy, long-horizon, real-world stuff is going to drive the next jump, and I think that's actually a more interesting problem than tuning one more algorithm.

So my answer is: yes, probably one model, but the path there is going to look less like "a bigger RL run" and more like "a lot of careful work on what we're even training it to do."

r001.rationale: The response discusses which tasks have clean environments and rewards, but does not state that reasoning transfer between tasks depends on the tasks’ nature.

r002.rationale: It says it is optimistic that one model can do all tasks and concludes, “yes, probably one model.”

r003.rationale: It says RL can appear to generalize, but attributes that to the stronger pretrained model and does not state that applying RL across many tasks enables transfer to additional tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s possible in principle, but reinforcement learning alone doesn’t guarantee that outcome. The key question is what tasks the model gets to practice, what feedback it receives, and whether what it learns transfers to new situations.

For a particular task with a clear reward, you can imagine training a very strong specialist. But putting many tasks together doesn’t automatically give you a generalist. Some tasks have conflicting objectives; others are difficult to evaluate at all. And even defining “all tasks” is tricky, because people keep inventing new ones.

So I would distinguish a model that already knows how to do everything from a model that can learn to do new things. The second seems more plausible to me. You could have a broadly capable model that uses tools, explores an environment, gets feedback, and adapts. Reinforcement learning could be an important part of building that ability, but the goal would be learning how to solve unfamiliar problems, rather than memorizing a solution for every possible task.

r001.rationale: It says transfer depends on which tasks the model practices and whether learning carries to new situations, and notes that tasks can differ in objectives and evaluability.

r002.rationale: It calls a single model performing all tasks possible in principle, while qualifying that reinforcement learning does not guarantee it.

r003.rationale: It connects task practice and transfer to new situations, then says reinforcement learning could help build a model that learns to solve unfamiliar problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by “all tasks.” If we mean a single model that can learn to handle a very broad range of tasks, that seems plausible. But if we mean one model that is already optimal at everything, I’m more skeptical. Different tasks have different constraints, and sometimes those constraints conflict.

Reinforcement learning gives us a way to improve through interaction, but the key question is: where do those interactions and rewards come from? For a task where you can reliably check success, the learning signal is relatively clear. For open-ended work, even defining success can be difficult. Having a general learning algorithm doesn’t automatically give you a general training environment.

So I’d distinguish a single model from a single intelligent system. You might have a model at the center, but it can use tools, maintain memory, and adapt to new environments. In that sense, generality may come less from putting every capability into fixed parameters and more from learning how to acquire the capabilities a task requires. Reinforcement learning could be an important part of that, but I wouldn’t assume that scaling it alone resolves the whole problem.

r001.rationale: The response notes that tasks have different constraints, but does not state that reasoning transfer between tasks depends on their nature.

r002.rationale: It says a single model that can learn to handle a very broad range of tasks seems plausible.

r003.rationale: It describes reinforcement learning as potentially important, but does not say that training across many tasks enables transfer to additional tasks.
